To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

intention to be vaccinated against pandemic swine influenza was predicted by attitude, subjective norm and perceived control, anticipating regret and the intention to receive a seasonal influenza vaccination, and that Black respondents were less likely to be vaccinated than Asian or White respondents.

The intention to vaccinate was influenced by the following: (1) the perceived benefits of vaccination (2) the perceived costs of vaccination (3) the perceived control over vaccination (4) the perceived social pressure to vaccinate (5) the anticipated feelings of regret for not having a vaccination (6) the intention to get a seasonal influenza vaccine this year (7) the perceived susceptibility to swine flu (8) the perceived severity of swine flu and (9) demographic variables.

the intention of adults to vaccinate against swine flu was predicted by attitude, subjective norm and perceived control, as well as anticipated regret, intention to have a flu vaccine, perceived barriers (not being bothered), and perceived benefits (decreased risk of swine flu and decreased frequency of consulting the doctor).
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how people make decisions to have or to not have a pandemic influenza vaccine.
identifying the key predictors of future vaccination intentions and the implications of this for public health policy.
understanding and predicting vaccination behaviour in adults in the UK.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Theory of Planned Behavior is a useful tool in understanding and predicting intention to vaccinate in the general population.
this study has demonstrated that the Theory of Planned Behavior is a useful framework for predicting intention to vaccinate for pandemic influenza.

this study found that the extended Theory of Planned Behavior model predicted 60% variance in the intention of adults in the United Kingdom to be vaccinated against pandemic swine influenza, and that the most important predictors of intention to be vaccinated were attitudes towards the vaccine, subjective norms, perceived control, the anticipated feelings of regret if one misses the opportunity to get vaccinated, intention to have a vaccination for seasonal influenza and two perceived benefits of being vaccinated against pandemic swive influenza.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Theory of Planned Behavior is an effective model for predicting vaccination intention, and that this theory could be applied in the development of future vaccination campaigns.
the Theory of Planned behaviour is a useful framework for identifying determinants that may influence vaccination decisions.

the extended Theory of Planned behaviour is useful in identifying determinants that may predict adults' intention to get vaccinated against pandemic influenza and can be used to develop interventions that will maximise future vaccination uptake.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a theory of planned behaviour model is useful for predicting intention to have a pandemic vaccination and that this can be extended to include additional factors.
it is important to consider the context of the pandemic and the population being targeted.
the Theory of Planned behaviour can be extended to explain intention to have a pandemic swine flu vaccination and that it can be used to inform the design of interventions to increase uptake.
